message: Hi [CLIENT_NAME_001]. I understand that you want to move quickly on an initial prototype. I’m fully comfortable taking care of both the mechanical and electrical aspects. Regarding mounting, I don’t anticipate needing metal mounting hardware for the motors themselves, since the torque should be handled easily. I’d be comfortable with a 3-4 week timeline.

Regarding your stability concerns, the unit will use a solid base and rubber/TPU feet so it does not rattle or shift around. The first build will be kept as simple as possible, with off-the-shelf components used for the electronics. Mixing should be reliable because we’ll select a motor that can easily manage the liquid load. I can provide a BOM within 24-48 hours.

Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001] — that sounds excellent, and I’m happy with both the approach and the timeline.

Let’s proceed.

For the initial step, I want to concentrate on:
• the system layout
• selection of the motor + components
• a basic wiring plan

The goal is to have a working prototype operating as soon as possible and refine it afterward.

Tell me what you need from me in order to begin.

Excellent, [CLIENT_NAME_001]. If you’re prepared to start, I am too. My final question concerns power: are you planning to plug this into a standard 120v wall outlet, or would you rather power it with 12v, like a car battery? If any additional questions come up, I’ll let you know promptly. I’m ready to start the CAD work and assemble a bill of materials. Everything on my side is set for us to proceed. Thank you; I’m looking forward to working with you on this project.

For the time being, let’s use a standard 120V wall outlet.

I’d like the first version to remain as straightforward and dependable as possible for events. Battery power can always be considered for a future version.

Everything is good from my side, and I’m excited to begin. As you start the CAD and BOM, let me know what you need from me.

That works, [CLIENT_NAME_004] use 120v, and it can be modified or adapted later for a 12v battery if necessary. I’ll start on the CAD and BOM now, and I can begin working today as soon as you send over the contract. I’m looking forward to it!
I’m preparing the contract now and will send it to you tomorrow. I’m looking forward to working together.
Thank you, [CLIENT_NAME_002] likewise looking forward to working with you.
Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001],
Attached please find the contract.

Hi [CLIENT_NAME_003] contract looks good, and I accept its terms. One note: to make everything official on upwork, you’ll need to submit it through their system using the hire button. You can revise the proposal I originally sent so that it includes your milestones.
Thank you, [FREELANCER_NAME_001]. This will be my first hire on Upwork, and I’m taking care of it now.
No worries. I completely understand.
When I select the Hire button, should I attach the contract there?
Yes, you can attach it there, but you should also enter the milestones in the official upwork one.
Can I upload the contract as an attachment in the first section, then? I noticed there was a separate tab for Milestones. Should I create another Milestones PDF and upload it in that section?

You can place the PDF in the first section, then enter the milestones from the contract in the following section. I’ve only performed work for other people through Upwork, so I’m not 100% certain what the hiring process looks like from your side.
Working on it now.
Thank you, [CLIENT_NAME_004] begin working on this for you and keep you informed of my progress.
Great! Thanks.
I expect to complete the initial BOM today. Afterward, I’ll create a rough CAD, but I’ll need to physically receive the components before I can establish the final measurements and exact positioning.

Okay. There’s one detail I forgot to bring up that occurred to me later. In the attached image of the matcha mixer, there is no actual way to pour the matcha. I’d like to add a spout at the bottom that faces the barista and makes pouring easy.
Is that practical to implement, or would another method work better?
That makes the design somewhat more complicated, but it should still be feasible.
Tricky? How so?

Unless I’m misunderstanding, you want the motor positioned beneath the bowl, with the mixing head extending through the bottom. My current plan is to make a hole directly in the bowl’s center for that mechanism. The drainage opening would need to be offset from it, which could leave some liquid at the bottom even after fully draining.
Can we work around that issue while keeping the process smooth and efficient?
If we revise the design to resemble this, A) would it pour more efficiently? B) would construction be simpler? C) would the timeframe change?

Yes, that design would improve pouring efficiency. It would also simplify the build because we would avoid the possible shaft-seal leakage associated with the other approach. Switching to a build like this should not negatively affect the time frame.

Okay, let’s use this design. It still preserves the DJ Turntables vibe. The pour spout should face the baristas, and I want the buttons to work and be functional. Let’s also make it as splash-free as possible. Keep the existing words on the machine, along with the green accents. The sole wording change is that it should read "[CLIENT_NAME_001]'s Matcha Mixer". I like the machine’s thickness in the side view. I want deep matcha wells without making the box overly large.

For the spout, I want to confirm the following:
• It has a clean open/close mechanism without dripping
• It is sealed correctly so nothing leaks into the base
• It can be cleaned easily between uses
• The pouring flow remains smooth and controlled

I’d like to know how you would implement those features in a straightforward, dependable way for V1.

Key Design Requirements
1\. Valve / flow control

I do not want:

continuous dripping
pouring that cannot be controlled

I need 👉

a straightforward open/close valve or tap

2\. Bottom seal

This is essential.

👉 The bowl must:

remain leak-free
not seep into electronics
3\. Cleaning

Matcha + milk leaves residue

👉 The spout needs to be:

removable OR
simple to flush/clean
4\. Flow rate

I do not want:

a slow drip
or an explosive pour

👉 The stream should be smooth and controlled

I’ll review everything you’ve provided, develop a new approach, and follow up shortly. There is one more design point I’d like to discuss: how much matcha does each bowl need to mix at once? At the moment, I’m considering 8qt bowls, which would let you mix approximately 6qt of matcha in each bowl. Is that close to the ideal capacity, or should I adjust it upward or downward for more or less?

I would actually rather use the smaller bowl size shown in the earlier design.

Refilling is not a concern because I want to prioritize:
• higher mixing quality
• consistent foam
• quicker visual cycles at events

For that reason, I’d favor less capacity per bowl instead of increasing to 8qt.
The attached picture demonstrates how 8 qt's would look. Bowls of that size detract from the design and its aesthetic. I’m fine with refilling, so let’s choose a smaller bowl size matching the earlier pictures.

One minor adjustment to think about

Because we’re choosing smaller bowls:

Please design them so they can be removed and swapped quickly.

This would allow me to pre-prep bowls and exchange them rapidly during events.
I’d also like the design to be beige. The bowl size shown here works for me.
understood.

I have the initial BOM prepared for your review, including the recent design details you raised. I already have materials in my shop for certain items, including extra wires, hardware, and the custom-fabricated housing. Those items will be included in the BOM later, once construction starts. I’ll now begin the preliminary cad design using approximate component dimensions. After you approve the components and authorize their purchase, I can take accurate measurements of every part and fully refine the design. I selected all components from amazon so we can iterate quickly if anything must be changed or added later.

Vessels: 2.5-Quart Stainless Steel Bowls (Qty 2), costing $16.82. These will function as the primary mixing reservoirs. Purchase link: [URL_001]

Motors: 12V 200RPM Gear Motors (Qty 2), costing $29.98. These are the high-speed drive units for mixing. Purchase link: [URL_002]

Drivetrain: 3/8" Shaft Couplings (Qty 2), costing $17.38. These join each motor to its extension shaft. Purchase link: [URL_003]

Drivetrain: 3/8" x 8" 304 Stainless Steel Shafts (Qty 2), costing $8.49. These extend from the motors to the whisks. Purchase link: [URL_004]

Agitators: Wire Whisks (Qty 2), costing $27.98. These mixing heads provide high aeration for frothing. Purchase link: [URL_005]

Control: PWM DC Speed Controllers (Qty 2), costing $16.99. These let the user adjust the vortex speed. Purchase link: [URL_006]

Power: 12V 20A DC Power Supply (Qty 1), costing $13.89. This supplies the main power for all electronics. Purchase link: [URL_007]

Cooling: 120mm 12V Cooling Fans (Qty 2), costing $11.99. These manage heat inside the enclosure. Purchase link: [URL_008]

Structural: Brass Bulkhead Fittings 3/8" F to 1/2" M (Qty 2), costing $11.99. These provide the through-bowl mounting point for the drive shaft. Purchase link: [URL_009]

Plumbing: 5/16" ID Silicone Tubing 10ft (Qty 1), costing $9.99. This forms the primary transfer lines between the bowls and spigots. Purchase link: [URL_010]

Adapters: SS 5/16" Barb to 3/4" GHT Female (Qty 2), costing $16.99. These adapt the tubing to the male threads on the spigots. Purchase link: [URL_011]

Coupling: 5/16" Barb Unions (Qty 2), costing $5.59. These create modular break-points to simplify cleaning. Purchase link: [URL_012]

Dispensing: Push-Style Beverage Spigots (Qty 2), costing $6.39. These provide the user-facing dispensing controls. Purchase link: [URL_013]

Sealing: #2 Silicone Stopper 5/16" Hole (Qty 5), costing $10.79. These create friction-fit seals at the bowl outlets to prevent leakage. Purchase link: [URL_014]

Connection: 5/16" Barb to 1/2" NPT Adapter (Qty 2), costing $8.49. These provide the rigid connection within each stopper. Purchase link: [URL_015]

The Estimated Component Total is $221.74.

Power comes from the 120v to 12v 20A Dc power supply, with separate PWM speed controllers. At each station, a 12v 200rpm motor attaches through a 3/8" shaft coupling to a 3/8" stainless steel shaft. That shaft drives the wire whisk used to blend and froth the matcha. The electronics receive cooling from 120mm fans. On the plumbing side, each 2.5 quart stainless steel bowl has a 5/16 barb outlet. A #2 silicone stopper provides a press-fit, leak-proof seal. The 5/16 silicone tubing travels from the barb union inside the stopper to the 3/4" ght adapter, which screws directly onto the push-style beverage spigots.

Certain details will be easier to understand visually after I complete the initial CAD, but I wanted you to see the anticipated materials now so you could raise any questions or recommend changes while I continue designing.
Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001],
The Whisker is oversized. We’ll be whisking fine powder, and although the bowls you’re purchasing are 2.5qt, those whiskers are intended for 6qt bowls. We need smaller, thinner ones.
Also, could the spout more closely match the diagram? I’m unsure whether Matcha will retain the same consistency after passing through a spout like that. It would lose its frothiness.
Here is the reference link: [URL_016]
Please treat this as a reference for the type of whisker we need. This style works better for whisking fine powder.

I understand the whisker concern and will locate a more appropriate component. Regarding the spout, the design in your image is possible, but it would involve custom work, another round of rethinking, and custom circuitry. We would essentially need a solenoid that opens and closes a valve inside the dispensing mechanism, allowing matcha to flow from that type of spout on demand. Developing a reliable mechanism and solution would require custom mechanical parts, wiring, and some r&d. It would probably extend beyond the timeline for this 1st edition. There are multiple off-the-shelf spout alternatives; might one of those work?
Here are the off-the-shelf spout options: [URL_017]
Hi [FREELANCER_NAME_001],
A spout is probably not the best option for dispensing the Matcha, since it would lose its consistency. Could we develop a gravity-based dispensing method instead?

I can make that work, although it represents a significant change to the engineering scope. Regarding the spout, I’m struggling to find an existing option that resembles the one shown in your renders. However, I found this spout and believe it would function well: [URL_018] A solenoid valve would sit directly beneath the bowl, preventing any matcha from reaching the spout until the button is pressed. Releasing the button would stop dispensing. Because no matcha would remain inside the spout or tubing, its frothiness should be preserved. Please take a look at this option. If you would rather retain the appearance of the spout from your original renders, I could fabricate a custom one, but it would not be steel.
Actually, after doing more research and thinking it over further, I believe I can fabricate the spouts myself from stainless steel and make them look very similar to the rendering you supplied.

Please move forward with that and match the render as closely as possible. I really like both the appearance and functionality shown in the render. There is also one change from the rendering: move the plate reading "[CLIENT_NAME_001]'s Matcha Mixer" from the back of the machine to the front. The spout and mixers will be positioned in front of the baristas, while customers will view the machine from another angle. I want "[CLIENT_NAME_001]'s Matcha Mixer" oriented toward the customer.
Will do. I’m almost done with the revised build approach and updated BOM.
Ok.

The revised build plan remains similar to the original, with some changes to accommodate the new spout and solenoid valve. A stainless steel bulkhead will screw into the opening at the bottom of the bowl. A stainless steel nipple will then attach to it, forming a quick-release setup so the bowls can be swapped easily. The nipple slides into a silicone plug to form a watertight seal, while the opposite side of that plug fits into the 1/2 inch 90 degree connector. That connector will attach to a solenoid valve, which will send the matcha to the stainless steel spout when a button is pressed.
For the whisks, I believe I can incorporate the exact ones you showed me. They are approximately 1/2 the size of the wire whisk originally planned, which should fit the 2.5qt bowls nicely.
Here is the newly proposed BOM:
Could you send me a mock-up showing the whisk design you plan to use?
My plan is to use the exact whisk you recommended from Amazon yesterday. Creating a small adapter that connects the steel mixing rod to that whisk should be fairly straightforward.

Hey [FREELANCER_NAME_001] — I reviewed the BOM, and I really like the overall direction. It matches what I was hoping for.

Before we proceed, I’d like your thoughts on a few items:

• Motors — I’m concerned that 200 RPM could be slightly too slow to produce a strong, frothy matcha texture. Would increasing the RPM make sense while still preserving enough torque for smooth mixing?

• Whisk — compared with the resin whisk, would a stainless steel or milk-frother-style head provide better consistency, durability, and foam quality?

• Spout — I want to continue with the solenoid solution. The pour needs to be clean, controlled, and seamless (mix → open → pour), both to protect the texture and create the right visual experience.

• Splash / mess control — this matters a lot for events. I want to ensure:
– little to no splashing while mixing
– a smooth, controlled stream from the spout without sputtering
– no drips after the valve closes
– effective seals so nothing leaks into the base
– a splash guard or lip around the bowl if one is necessary

• Cleaning — if possible, the bowls and spout parts should either be removable or otherwise easy to clean.

I’m happy with everything else. I’d like to know what you think about these points and whether you would change anything before we finalize the BOM.

Regarding the motors, I think your concern about speed is correct. I’ve chosen new motors rated for 1000RPM. The PWM controller will continue to provide adjustment from 0 through 1000 while preserving enough torque to mix the liquids.

The whisk is more complicated because there are not many choices that meet our requirements. We need a reasonably large mixing head so the entire bowl mixes properly. The bowl measures approximately 9 inch across, but the plastic mixing head listed on the BOM is only about 2.4" in diameter. By comparison, the original wire whisk I proposed measured around 4.5" in diameter. Although it is advertised for a 6qt bowl, I believe it could still perform well in our smaller bowl. Ideally, the head would resemble those used on handheld electric frothers/mixers, but those are only available in very small sizes.

I do not expect splashing to be a problem. If the mixing becomes too vigorous, the motor speed can be adjusted while it is running. Should splashing occur, we can add the simple splash guard you suggested.

For cleaning, the current design makes the bowl very easy to remove. I also intend to make the custom spout removable so it can be cleaned easily.

Overall, I believe we are almost ready. I’ll update the motor to 1000rpm. For the whisk, perhaps we should choose 2 styles and test them to determine which performs best. The whisk should be among the easiest parts to exchange for a different design if necessary, since a basic adapter should allow nearly any whisk to connect to our setup.

I found another whisk that might work. It has the same diameter as the resin whisk from amazon, but it is stainless steel. I could remove its handle and adapt the remaining portion to the shaft. [URL_019]
That whisk will work. For the motor speed, let’s also set the maximum at 1500. What are your thoughts?
Yea, of course. We can restrict the speed using the knobs, and the extra capacity will give us some flexibility while testing to find the right setting.
Great.

I’m having difficulty locating a suitable motor in the 1500 range, so I recommend using these motors rated at 3000RPM. Their RPM will remain fully adjustable from 0 through the maximum of 3000rpm. They are slightly larger than the previously proposed motors and should withstand prolonged use better. Their shafts can also be cut down to the required length. [URL_020]
The CAD work is still at a very early stage. I will refine the sharp angles and other details.

That reasoning makes sense. I like having additional power while still being able to control the available speed range.

I’m comfortable with 3000 RPM as long as the motors are not constantly operated at maximum speed. Being able to tune them for different mixing intensities, such as a slow mix versus higher-speed frothing, would actually be ideal.

With the higher RPM, I want to ensure that:
• splashing remains controlled
• mixing stays smooth rather than becoming overly aggressive at higher speeds

If necessary, I’m open to incorporating a splash guard or adjusting the whisk position / bowl depth so the machine operates cleanly.

Overall, I approve of this direction.
Based on the CAD images of the base, are the whiskers going to be removable?

The whiskers will be removable. The motor mounting height has not been finalized yet, and it will probably need to be raised somewhat to provide clearance for removing the bowl and related components.
Great.

As you continue refining the layout, there are several details I want us to get right:

• Bowl removal — the bowls should lift out easily without being obstructed by the whisk or motor assembly.

• Whisk removal — ideally, detaching it should be fast and straightforward, without tools if possible, because cleaning and swapping parts during events will matter.

• Whisk positioning — setting the correct height will be important for producing good foam and limiting splashes, particularly with the higher RPM range.

• Splash control — because we selected a more powerful motor, the machine needs to remain clean while operating, whether that is achieved through positioning, bowl geometry, or a discreet guard if required.

Everything looks great so far. I just want these usability details optimized for actual event use.

I’m presently considering a straightforward "twist lock" mechanism for the whisk. Easy whisk removal will be essential for taking out the bowl because the whisker will sit directly in the bowl’s removal path. Standard mixers address this by using a mixing head that tilts upward. I’ll experiment with multiple whisk heights and depths to determine which position delivers the best and most consistent mixing results.
Great.

Will you be sending an updated BOM? Also, what is your preferred way to handle payment for the BOM? Should I purchase all the items and ship them to you, or will the address associated with the links automatically direct the orders to you?
I’ll put together and send the revised BOM. Either arrangement works for me, so we can use whichever option you find easiest and most comfortable.
If that works for you, I can buy the parts myself. Doing so would make any necessary exchanges or substitutions somewhat easier. The cost could be included in the milestone or provided as a tip.
Finalized BOM:
The most efficient approach would be for you to purchase the parts and have me reimburse you. I’m reviewing the BOM now; once I approve the materials, you can place the orders.

Hey [FREELANCER_NAME_001] — I reviewed the finalized BOM, and everything looks very solid. I’m very happy with the direction, and it seems like we’re close to finalizing it.

Before I proceed with ordering the parts, I have a few final points to verify:

• Motors — the listing refers to an eccentric output shaft. Can you confirm whether the whisk will still rotate smoothly and remain centered, or whether a straight/centered shaft would provide better stability?

• Motor performance — moving to 3000 RPM gives us useful flexibility. I just want to confirm that we can tune the speed for smooth mixing without creating excessive splashing at the higher settings.

• Solenoid flow — because the valves are on/off, do you expect them to open with a smooth pour, or could the liquid release too suddenly? I want a clean, controlled pour that does not splash.

• Power supply — under load, does the 12V 20A power supply comfortably support both motors, the solenoids, and the fans at the same time?

• Splash control — given the higher RPM, can whisk placement, bowl depth, and the overall configuration keep operation clean? For events, I want the machine to be as splash-proof and mess-free as possible.

Everything else looks excellent. I just want these points fully resolved before the order is submitted.

Let me know what you think.
One more question about the spouts: you mentioned that you would fabricate them yourself, correct? I don’t see them listed on the BOM.

Regarding the motors, the reference to an eccentric output shaft was actually leftover text from the motor selected previously. The new motor uses a centered shaft.

The solenoid should provide a smooth flow. Its 1/2 outlet should keep the liquids from discharging abruptly.

It would probably be prudent to upgrade to a power supply with higher output. That would lower the chance of overheating or overloading. Higher-rated PWM controllers would also be helpful for the same overheating concern.

As for the spouts, I will fabricate them from 1/32 stainless steel. The material is listed at the very bottom of the BOM.
I’ll replace the parts we discussed with higher-power alternatives.

Here is the newly revised BOM. The only changes from the prior version are that the PWM motor controllers were replaced with higher-power units and the AC/DC adapter was upgraded to a 50A model. That version should provide more than sufficient power, including reserve capacity, to prevent overheating. I also rechecked all pricing because there were several differences between the amounts I had recorded and the current prices.

Everything looks great, and I’m ready for the ordering process to begin.

I just want to verify one final point: all listed components are fully compatible with each other, including the motor shafts, couplings, controllers, and power configuration, correct?

After you confirm that, please place the order and have all items delivered to you. I’ll reimburse you.

Hey [CLIENT_NAME_001], yes, every listed item is fully compatible with the other components. That includes both the power-related equipment and the mechanical parts, such as the shafts, couplings, and so on.

Does this show only the machine, or does it include the attached base? The two rectangular openings along the bottom appear to be spouts; what are the circles positioned above them? The two openings on top seem to be whisk adjusters, but what is the third smaller opening for? Also, where will the power button be located?
